claims.text: S1's SLO in slo.md is 99.5% of order requests (POST api/v1/orders and api/v2/orders) not answered with a 5xx, over a rolling 28-day window.

Error budget = the share of events an SLO allows to be bad over its window, 1 minus the target, counted in requests; assumed example: 200,000 order requests in 28 days at 99.5% gives 1,000 failed requests.

slo.md policy, agreed in advance by team and product owner, not re-argued during a failure: budget left -> release as usual; a failing release spends budget like any failure; budget spent -> feature releases stop, only fixes and reliability work until the SLI is back above the SLO.
S1 counts every 5xx to the order endpoints regardless of cause (the PromQL selects code!~"5.." only); a revert stops further failures but the failures already counted stay in the window.
With a rolling window, the SLI returns above the SLO as new good requests arrive and old failures fall out of the last 28 days.

0.5% of under 200 requests is under one; with under 800 order requests in the hour, four 500s exceed the budget, so budget left goes below zero. 1,000 / 4 = 250. $orders (script line 27) holds the order labels; [1h] since the lab holds far less than 28 days of data.

slo.md states, in its scope section, what it does not count, such as requests that fail at Caddy or the Gateway before reaching the API.

claims.text: While budget remains, a team may spend it on risky changes such as releases; a team that never spends any is likely holding back changes it could ship, and is being more careful than its SLO asks.

Trade-offs of budget policies: no written policy (argument each time), policy agreed in advance (one rule, features may wait), stop every release (fixes wait too), count only the team's own failures (blame arguments; customers felt them anyway).

When the budget is spent and the product owner wants a feature, hold it and change the policy afterwards if needed; when a dependency (db) spent it, the policy still applies and the reliability work concerns how the api behaves without PostgreSQL.
Missing the SLO is the problem, spending part of the budget below it is not; a team afraid to spend any tends to ship less often, in larger batches that carry more risk each.
